html:
A round tomb on the Via Nomentana, just outside the ancient walls of Rome, built for Constantina, daughter of Constantine the Great, who died in 354. It was long dated to Constantine's reign; excavations in 1992 point to about 350. It stood against the side of a huge funeral hall begun from 338 over the catacomb where the martyr Saint Agnes was believed to lie, since early Christians wanted to be buried close to martyrs. The hall is now a ruin, but the tomb survives almost whole, one of the best kept buildings of late antiquity in Rome.

The plan is a ring inside a ring. A high central space, lit by twelve windows in a drum under a shallow dome, stands on twelve pairs of granite columns, and around it runs a darker barrel-vaulted walkway. The vault of the walkway keeps its 4th-century mosaics, made of small marble pieces on a pale ground: vines, birds, vessels, geometric patterns, and cupids picking grapes and treading them into wine. The scenes are hardly Christian at all, and in the Renaissance the building was taken for a temple of Bacchus. Two small apses hold mosaics of Christ, among them Christ giving the law to Peter, made later, probably in the 5th or 7th century. The dome mosaic is lost and known only from 16th-century watercolours, and the coloured marble of the walls is gone.

Constantina's great porphyry sarcophagus, or her sister Helena's, carved with the same wine harvest, is now in the Vatican Museums. Pope Nicholas I said mass here in 865, the first time the name Santa Costanza is recorded, and Pope Alexander IV consecrated it as a church in 1254. Its round plan, centred on the person honoured, is the plan of the other imperial tombs of the time, such as Diocletian's in his palace at Split and the Rotunda of Galerius at Thessaloniki.
